obf4.what:
Observability maturity model: level 0 (no instrumentation) → level 1 (basic metrics) → level 2 (pillars implemented) → level 3 (correlated telemetry) → level 4 (self-service, AI-assisted).
  • Level 0 — Dark: no instrumentation, SSH into servers, console.log debugging
  • Level 1 — Basic: infrastructure metrics (CPU/memory/disk), simple uptime monitoring
  • Level 2 — Instrumented: structured logging, RED metrics, basic tracing on critical paths
  • Level 3 — Correlated: OpenTelemetry, trace-log-metric correlation, SLO-based alerting
  • Level 4 — Proactive: AI-driven anomaly detection, auto-remediation, self-service observability platform
  • Most orgs sit at Level 2 — reaching Level 3 is the architect-level differentiator

obf1.desc: Observability is the ability to measure the internal state of a system by examining its outputs (logs, metrics, traces). It answers "what is happening?" without deploying new code. Originated from control theory: a syste
obf1.what:
Observability is the ability to measure the internal state of a system by examining its outputs (logs, metrics, traces). It answers "what is happening?" without deploying new code.
  • Originated from control theory: a system is observable if you can infer internal state from external outputs
  • Three pillars: logs (discrete events), metrics (aggregated data), traces (request lifecycle)
  • Observability != monitoring — monitoring tells you something is wrong, observability tells you WHY
  • Enables debugging of unknown-unknowns: failures you didn't anticipate or define alert rules for
  • Key metric: MTTD (Mean Time to Detect) vs MTTR (Mean Time to Resolve) — observability reduces both
  • High-cardinality data (user IDs, request IDs) is essential for effective observability
obf1.why: Observability separates reactive firefighting from proactive system understanding — it's the foundation of running distributed systems in production.

obf3.desc: Cardinality refers to the number of unique values a label/tag dimension can have. Low cardinality: HTTP methods (GET/POST). High cardinality: user IDs, request IDs. Low cardinality ( Medium cardinality ( High cardinality
obf3.what:
Cardinality refers to the number of unique values a label/tag dimension can have. Low cardinality: HTTP methods (GET/POST). High cardinality: user IDs, request IDs.
  • Low cardinality (<100 values): HTTP status codes, deployment versions, availability zones
  • Medium cardinality (<10K values): service names, endpoint paths, error codes
  • High cardinality (millions): user IDs, session IDs, request IDs, IP addresses
  • Metrics engines (Prometheus) struggle with high cardinality — cardinality explosion kills performance
  • Tracing naturally handles high cardinality via span IDs and trace IDs
  • Strategy: use metrics for low-cardinality aggregations, traces for high-cardinality investigations
obf3.why: Cardinality is the #1 performance bottleneck in observability — choosing wrong dimensions makes systems slower or too expensive.

obf2.what:
Monitoring watches known failure modes with predefined dashboards and alerts. Observability enables ad-hoc investigation of any system behavior.
  • Monitoring: black box — observe system from outside, check predefined health indicators
  • Observability: white box — instrument the system to expose internal state for exploration
  • Monitoring answers "is it working?" — observability answers "why isn't it working?"
  • Monitoring creates known-knowns — observability surfaces unknown-unknowns
  • Production: both are needed — monitoring for alerting, observability for root cause analysis
  • Shift: move from "what can we monitor?" to "what questions will we need to answer?"
obf2.why: The distinction determines your entire operations strategy — monitoring-only leaves you blind to novel failures.

obf5.name: The Three Pillars deep dive: logs, metrics, traces
obf5.desc: Each pillar serves a different purpose: logs tell a story (what happened), metrics show trends (how many), traces map causality (where in the request flow). Logs: high verbosity, structured JSON, contain detailed context
obf5.what:
Each pillar serves a different purpose: logs tell a story (what happened), metrics show trends (how many), traces map causality (where in the request flow).
  • Logs: high verbosity, structured JSON, contain detailed context — expensive to store and query at scale
  • Metrics: lightweight, numeric, aggregated over time windows — lose individual request detail
  • Traces: capture request flow across services — provide causality but have sampling overhead
  • The pillars are not mutually exclusive — correlation between them is the real power
  • OpenTelemetry unifies all three: traces carry context, metrics aggregate, logs attach to spans
  • Analogy: logs = witness testimony, metrics = security camera summary, traces = surveillance footage
obf5.why: Understanding when to use each pillar (and their limitations) is the core skill of observability — no single pillar suffices.

olo1.what:
Structured logging emits machine-parseable records (JSON) with consistent fields. Unstructured logging emits free-text strings that require regex to extract meaning.
  • Structured: {"level":"error","msg":"request failed","status":503,"duration_ms":4500,"trace_id":"abc123"}
  • Unstructured: "ERROR: request failed - took 4500ms" — needs regex to parse, fragile to format changes
  • JSON is the standard format — supports nested objects, arrays, and mixed types
  • Pino: fastest Node.js logger (~5x faster than Winston) with native JSON support
  • Logs should have: timestamp, level, message, service, trace_id, span_id, and domain-specific fields
  • Avoid logging PII, secrets, or large payloads — use log redaction and sampling
olo1.why: Structured logging is the baseline for any serious production system — unstructured logs are nearly impossible to query at scale.

olo3.desc: Centralized logging aggregates logs from all services into a searchable store. ELK (Elasticsearch, Logstash, Kibana) and Grafana Loki are the dominant stacks. ELK stack: Logstash parses/ships → Elasticsearch indexes → Ki
olo3.what:
Centralized logging aggregates logs from all services into a searchable store. ELK (Elasticsearch, Logstash, Kibana) and Grafana Loki are the dominant stacks.
  • ELK stack: Logstash parses/ships → Elasticsearch indexes → Kibana visualizes
  • Grafana Loki: push-based, stores compressed logs, indexes by labels (not full-text)
  • Log shipping agents: Filebeat (ELK), Promtail (Loki), Fluentd/Fluent Bit (vendor-neutral)
  • Logstash is heavy — Fluent Bit is preferred for edge/agent-side log collection
  • Loki is cheaper for high-volume logs (no full-text indexing) but limited query capabilities
  • Hot/warm/cold tiering: recent logs in fast storage (SSD), older in object storage (S3/GCS)

olo4.desc: Correlation IDs (trace IDs) propagate across service boundaries to stitch together logs from a single request. Each service logs the same trace_id. Generate correlation ID at ingress (API gateway or load balancer) Propag
olo4.what:
Correlation IDs (trace IDs) propagate across service boundaries to stitch together logs from a single request. Each service logs the same trace_id.
  • Generate correlation ID at ingress (API gateway or load balancer)
  • Propagate via HTTP headers: x-request-id, x-correlation-id, or traceparent (W3C)
  • Each service extracts the ID and includes it in all log statements
  • AsyncLocalStorage (Node.js) scopes correlation ID per request across async boundaries
  • Aggregation: query "trace_id=abc123" across all services → single timeline view
  • Tools: Elastic APM, Grafana Tempo, Datadog trace-log correlation
olo4.why: Without correlation IDs, debugging a multi-service request requires manual log spelunking across disparate sources — it's the #1 productivity booster.

ome1.what:
Counter (monotonically increasing), Gauge (up/down), Histogram (distribution of values), Summary (pre-computed quantiles). Each serves a different analytical purpose.
  • Counter: only increases or resets to 0 — request count, errors, bytes sent. Use rate() to derive per-second
  • Gauge: goes up and down — memory usage, active connections, queue depth
  • Histogram: bucket-based distribution of observed values — request latency, response size
  • Histogram provides: count, sum, bucket counts — derive p50/p95/p99 via histogram_quantile()
  • Summary: pre-computed quantiles on the client side — less flexible but more accurate
  • Prometheus best practice: use Histogram over Summary — server-side quantile calculation is more flexible
ome1.why: Choosing the wrong metric type leads to incorrect analysis — counters vs gauges is a classic interview distinction.

ome3.desc: Prometheus scrapes metrics from instrumented targets via HTTP pull model. Grafana visualizes Prometheus data with dashboards. Prometheus: pull-based — scrapes /metrics endpoints at configurable intervals (default 15s) from
ome3.why: Prometheus + Grafana is the industry standard — knowing PromQL and dashboard design is expected at the architect level.

ome5.desc: Google SRE's four universal signals: Latency (time to serve), Traffic (demand volume), Errors (failure rate), Saturation (how full the service is). Latency: distinguish between success and error latency — slow errors mask fast successes
ome5.what:
Google SRE's four universal signals: Latency (time to serve), Traffic (demand volume), Errors (failure rate), Saturation (how full the service is).
  • Latency: distinguish between success and error latency — slow errors mask fast successes
  • Traffic: requests/sec for HTTP, data rate for databases, concurrent users for real-time
  • Errors: explicit errors (5xx), implicit errors (200 with wrong answer), degradation (slow responses)
  • Saturation: CPU, memory, disk I/O, network — also dependencies like connection pool exhaustion
  • Usage: create a "Four Golden Signals" dashboard per service — the first thing to check during an incident
  • Threshold: alert when any signal crosses a predefined threshold — correlate signals during root cause
ome5.why: The Golden Signals are the smallest set of metrics that give a comprehensive view of any service — a classic SRE interview topic.

otr1.what:
A trace is a tree of spans. Each span represents a unit of work (an API call, a DB query). Spans carry: trace_id, span_id, parent_span_id, timestamps, attributes.
  • Trace = entire request lifecycle across all services, Span = single operation within the trace
  • Trace_id identifies the entire trace — Span_id identifies the specific span
  • Parent_span_id creates the tree structure — root span has no parent
  • W3C Trace Context: traceparent header (version-trace_id-span_id-trace_flags)
  • Propagation: service extracts trace context from incoming request → creates child span → passes to downstream
  • Span attributes: service name, operation name, HTTP method, status code, duration, custom tags
otr1.why: Distributed tracing is the ONLY way to understand request flow across microservices — essential for debugging latency and failures.

otr2.desc: Sampling decides which traces to store. Head-based: sample at request entry. Tail-based: sample after seeing the full trace. Probabilistic: random percentage. Head-based sampling: decide at the root span — simple but mis
otr2.what:
Sampling decides which traces to store. Head-based: sample at request entry. Tail-based: sample after seeing the full trace. Probabilistic: random percentage.
  • Head-based sampling: decide at the root span — simple but misses errors that happen deep in the trace
  • Tail-based sampling: buffer all traces, decide at the end — captures all errors but requires more memory
  • Probabilistic sampling: random X% — unbiased but may miss rare events entirely
  • Smart sampling: always sample errors (anywhere in trace), sample slow traces, probabilistic for healthy ones
  • Rate limiting: max traces/second to avoid overwhelming the backend
  • OpenTelemetry Collector supports tail-based sampling via the tail_sampling processor

otr3.desc: OpenTelemetry (OTel) is the vendor-neutral standard for instrumenting applications. SDK generates telemetry, Collector processes and exports to backends. OTel SDK: auto-instrumentation (zero-code via agent/hook) + manual
otr3.what:
OpenTelemetry (OTel) is the vendor-neutral standard for instrumenting applications. SDK generates telemetry, Collector processes and exports to backends.
  • OTel SDK: auto-instrumentation (zero-code via agent/hook) + manual instrumentation (via API)
  • OTel Collector: receivers (OTLP, Jaeger, Prometheus) → processors (batch, filter, sample) → exporters
  • OTLP protocol: binary, efficient, gRPC-based — the native protocol for OTel data exchange
  • Processors: batch (aggregate before export), attributes (add/remove tags), sampling (head/tail)
  • Exporters: send to any backend — Jaeger, Zipkin, Prometheus, Datadog, Grafana, self-hosted
  • OTel is CNCF graduated — it is the Linux Foundation of observability
otr3.why: OpenTelemetry is the industry standard — it replaces vendor-specific agents and gives you a unified instrumentation API.

otr4.desc: Jaeger (CNCF graduated, Go) and Zipkin (Finagle, Java) are the two dominant open-source tracing backends. They store traces and provide search/visualization UIs. Jaeger: Uber-born, Go, supports Elasticsearch/Cassandra/ba
otr4.what:
Jaeger (CNCF graduated, Go) and Zipkin (Finagle, Java) are the two dominant open-source tracing backends. They store traces and provide search/visualization UIs.
  • Jaeger: Uber-born, Go, supports Elasticsearch/Cassandra/badger storage, has deep dependency graph
  • Zipkin: Twitter-born, Java, supports Elasticsearch/Cassandra, simpler but less feature-rich
  • Jaeger UI: trace search by service/operation/tags, timeline view, flame graph, span details
  • Jaeger architecture: agent (sidecar) → collector → storage → query service → UI
  • Both support gRPC for trace ingestion and Web UI for trace exploration
  • OTel Collector can export to both: no need to choose between Jaeger and Zipkin

otr5.desc: The observability trifecta: logs reference trace_id, traces reference metric aggregations, metrics alert on anomaly that initiated the trace. All three linked for drill-down. Logs include trace_id and span_id in every st
otr5.what:
The observability trifecta: logs reference trace_id, traces reference metric aggregations, metrics alert on anomaly that initiated the trace. All three linked for drill-down.
  • Logs include trace_id and span_id in every structured log line — query "trace_id=abc" to see all logs
  • Metrics have label dimensions that map to service/operation — drill from metric to trace via exemplars
  • Exemplars: Prometheus feature that attaches a representative trace_id to a metric data point
  • Grafana Tempo: trace DB that integrates with Loki (logs) and Prometheus (metrics) for single-pane correlation
  • Workflow: Alert → metric graph → click exemplar → open trace → expand span → view associated logs
  • OpenTelemetry: logs emitted from within a span context automatically inherit trace_id and span_id
otr5.why: Correlation is the difference between having three tools and having ONE observability platform — it's what enables rapid root cause analysis.

oal2.desc: Alert fatigue occurs when teams receive too many irrelevant alerts. Solutions: grouping related alerts, silencing during maintenance, routing to the correct team. Grouping: Alertmanager groups similar alerts by labels (s
oal2.what:
Alert fatigue occurs when teams receive too many irrelevant alerts. Solutions: grouping related alerts, silencing during maintenance, routing to the correct team.
  • Grouping: Alertmanager groups similar alerts by labels (service, severity) into a single notification
  • Silencing: suppress alerts during deployments, maintenance windows, or known issues
  • Routing: route by severity (critical→PagerDuty, warning→Slack, info→dashboard)
  • Inhibition: higher-severity alert inhibits lower-severity alerts for the same service
  • Time-based: different routing on-call vs daytime — critical alerts always page, non-critical wait
  • Target: <5 alerts per on-call shift should require human action — everything else is noise
oal2.why: Alert fatigue is the #1 cause of missed critical incidents — if everything is urgent, nothing is urgent.

oal3.what:
On-call rotations distribute incident responsibility. Escalation policies define who gets paged when primary doesn't respond. Tiers route by severity.
  • Rotation: weekly or bi-weekly shifts — avoid frequent rotation (disrupts focus) and infrequent (rusty skills)
  • Follow-the-sun: rotate across timezone teams for 24h coverage without waking people at night
  • Tiers: L1 (initial triage), L2 (deep debugging), L3 (subject matter expert) — escalate up
  • Escalation: primary doesn't ack in N minutes → secondary → manager — auto-escalate, no manual intervention
  • Notification: PagerDuty/OpsGenie for critical (phone call), Slack for warning, email for info
  • Post-incident always: review if paging was appropriate — adjust rules based on false positives
oal3.why: Well-designed on-call processes prevent burnout and ensure incidents get the right attention — poorly designed ones lose engineers.

oal4.what:
Incident response is a structured process: detect → triage → mitigate → resolve → postmortem. Runbooks provide step-by-step remediation procedures.
  • IR phases: Detection → Triage (severity, assignee) → Mitigation (stop the bleeding) → Resolution (fix root cause) → Postmortem
  • Runbook: "What to do when [incident]" — includes dashboard links, debugging commands, rollback procedures
  • Blameless postmortem: focus on system/process failures, not individual mistakes — root cause = systemic cause
  • SLO tracking: was this incident within our error budget? Did we miss our SLO?
  • Action items: postmortem must produce concrete, tracked actions — "add alarm for X" not "monitor better"
  • Practice: game days and chaos engineering prepare teams for incidents before they happen in production

osc1.desc: OpenTelemetry is the CNCF observability framework. It includes specification, SDKs in all major languages, Collector for processing/routing, and OTLP wire protocol. OTel specification: signals (traces/metrics/logs), cont
osc1.what:
OpenTelemetry is the CNCF observability framework. It includes specification, SDKs in all major languages, Collector for processing/routing, and OTLP wire protocol.
  • OTel specification: signals (traces/metrics/logs), context propagation, semantic conventions
  • SDKs: Go, Java, JS/TS, Python, .NET, Ruby, PHP, C++ — auto-instrumentation where available
  • OTel Collector: receiver (OTLP, Prometheus, Jaeger, Kafka) → processor → exporter (any backend)
  • OTLP protocol: protobuf over gRPC, supports compression, batching, and retries
  • Semantic conventions: standardized attribute names (http.method, db.system, cloud.provider)
  • OTel is CNCF graduated + W3C trace context — it's the Linux Foundation of observability
osc1.why: OTel is the de facto industry standard — vendor-neutral instrumentation means you're never locked into a proprietary agent.

osc3.why: Self-service observability scales engineering without growing the platform team — developers instrument their own services correctly.

osc4.why: Retrofitting observability is 10x more expensive than building it in — making it part of dev workflow is the only scalable approach.

ope1.why: Profiling answers "where is CPU time actually spent?" — it's the only way to find real performance bottlenecks vs imagined ones.

ope2.why: Memory leaks in production cause OOM crashes — heap profiling is the only reliable way to find root cause.

ope3.desc: eBPF (extended Berkeley Packet Filter) runs sandboxed programs in the kernel without modifying kernel source. It hooks into syscalls, network events, and kernel functions for deep observability. eBPF programs run in kern
ope3.what:
eBPF (extended Berkeley Packet Filter) runs sandboxed programs in the kernel without modifying kernel source. It hooks into syscalls, network events, and kernel functions for deep observability.
  • eBPF programs run in kernel space in a safe sandbox (verifier ensures no crashes)
  • Hook points: syscalls, kprobes, tracepoints, network events (XDP, TC)
  • Use cases: network monitoring (Cilium), security (Falco), tracing (bpftrace), profiling (Pixie)
  • bpftrace: one-liner tracing language — bpftrace -e 'tracepoint:syscalls:sys_enter_* { @[comm] = count(); }'
  • Cilium: CNI for Kubernetes using eBPF for networking, service mesh, and network policy
  • Overhead: <1% CPU for most eBPF programs — far lower than traditional agents
ope3.why: eBPF provides kernel-level observability with near-zero overhead — it's the most powerful observability technology of the decade.

ofe1.why: Backend metrics can show 200 OK while users experience broken UIs — frontend observability closes the observability gap.

ofe3.desc: APM is the practice of monitoring application performance end-to-end. It combines metrics (latency, throughput, error rate), traces (request flow), and logs into a unified view. APM agents auto-instrument code and collec
ofe3.what:
APM is the practice of monitoring application performance end-to-end. It combines metrics (latency, throughput, error rate), traces (request flow), and logs into a unified view. APM agents auto-instrument code and collect telemetry.
  • APM pillars: metrics (RED/USE), distributed traces, logs, errors, and real user data
  • Auto-instrumentation: APM agents inject tracing/logging without code changes (Datadog agent, New Relic agent)
  • Service maps: auto-generated dependency graphs from trace data — shows which services talk to each other
  • Transaction tracing: capture a single request across all services, show time spent in each
  • Baselines: APM tools learn normal behavior and alert on anomalies (not static thresholds)
  • APM vs observability: APM is a tool category, observability is a property — APM helps achieve observability
ofe3.why: APM provides the big picture — from user click to database query — making it the primary tool for performance diagnosis.
